title: William Ewart Gladstone
wiki_lead:
William Ewart Gladstone (  YOO-ərt GLAD-stən; 29 December 1809 – 19 May 1898) was a British statesman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom for four non-consecutive terms between 1868 and 1894, the most of any British prime minister. He began in politics as a Conservative Member of Parliament (MP) for Newark and ended as the face of the Liberal Party. He also served four times as Chancellor of the Exchequer, five times as Leader of the House of Commons, and MP for over 60 years, from 1832 to 1846 and from 1847 to 1895, representing a total of five constituencies. His political career thus spanned nearly the entire Victorian era.
Gladstone was born in Liverpool to the prominent Scottish merchant and slaveholder Sir John Gladstone. A graduate of Eton and Oxford, Gladstone first entered the House of Commons in 1832 as a High Tory, a grouping that joined the Conservative Party under Sir Robert Peel in 1834. Gladstone served as a minister in both of Peel's governments, and in 1846 joined the breakaway Peelite faction that merged into the new Liberal Party in 1859. He was chancellor under Lord Aberdeen (1852–1855), Lord Palmerston (1859–1865) and Lord Russell (1865–1866). Gladstone's own political doctrine – which promoted equality of opportunity and the repeal of taxes and protectionist trade barriers – came to be known as Gladstonian liberalism. 
In 1868, Gladstone became prime minister for the first time. His ministry passed many reforms, including the disestablishment of the Church of Ireland and the introduction of secret voting. After electoral defeat in 1874, Gladstone resigned as leader of the Liberal Party. From 1876 he began a comeback based on moral opposition to the Ottoman Empire's massacres of Bulgarians. Gladstone's Midlothian speaking campaign of 1879–1880 is considered the first modern political campaign in Britain, and his popularity among the working class earned him the sobriquet "The People's William". After the 1880 general election, Gladstone returned as party leader and formed his second ministry (1880–1885), which saw the passage of the Third Reform Act as well as crises in Ireland — where his government passed repressive measures but also improved the legal rights of tenant farmers — and Egypt, where public outrage at the death of General Gordon in the Siege of Khartoum forced him to resign.
Gladstone's brief 1886 premiership was dominated by his proposal of home rule for Ireland that was defeated in the House of Commons and caused Liberal Unionists to break from his party. This helped keep the Liberals out of office for 20 years, barring the minority cabinet Gladstone formed in 1892. This time, the Government of Ireland Bill 1893 passed through the Commons but was defeated by a wide margin in the House of Lords. Gladstone resigned in March 1894, aged 84, as the oldest ever prime minister. His successor, Lord Rosebery, was defeated in a landslide in the subsequent year's election. Gladstone left Parliament in 1895 and died three years later.
A powerful orator, Gladstone was called by some the "G.O.M." (to his supporters, the "Grand Old Man"; to his rivals, "God's Only Mistake"). Historians often rank Gladstone as one of the greatest prime ministers in British history. His devoutness, charitable work (particularly with fallen women) and nonfiction texts on subjects ranging from the Oxford Movement to classical civilisation have also attracted attention.

Early life
William Ewart Gladstone was born on 29 December 1809 at 62 Rodney Street in Liverpool, the fourth son of Sir John Gladstone, a wealthy Scottish merchant, slave owner, planter and Tory politician; and his second wife, Anne MacKenzie Robertson. He was named after a close friend of his father, William Ewart, another Liverpool merchant and the father of William Ewart, later a Liberal politician. grok_lead: William Ewart Gladstone (29 December 1809 â 19 May 1898) was a British statesman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom for four non-consecutive terms, more than any other individual, leading Liberal governments focused on domestic reforms and imperial policy. Born in Liverpool to a wealthy merchant family with ties to the slave trade, Gladstone entered Parliament as a Tory MP in 1832, initially defending traditional Anglican establishment and opposing early abolitionist measures influenced by his father's slave-owning plantations. Shifting toward Peelite liberalism under Robert Peel, he championed free trade as Chancellor of the Exchequer, delivering landmark budgets that reduced tariffs and funded public works through fiscal prudence. His first ministry (1868â1874) achieved the disestablishment of the Church of Ireland, secret ballot in elections, and reforms in education, the army, and civil service, expanding public access and efficiency. Subsequent terms advanced Irish land rights against absentee landlords and broadened the electorate via the Representation of the People Act 1884, though his pursuit of Irish Home Rule in 1886 split the Liberal Party and alienated Queen Victoria, who viewed him as a volatile agitator. Gladstone's moral fervorâevident in his agitation against Ottoman atrocities in Bulgaria and personal nocturnal missions to rescue London prostitutesâcoexisted with pragmatic governance, earning him the moniker "Grand Old Man" amid criticisms like "Murderer of Gordon" for perceived hesitancy in Sudan.
